ideas.hypothesis: IPO first-day abnormal returns are larger and reverse more slowly for Shenzhen-listed stocks than Shanghai-listed stocks, because Shenzhen returns show stronger long memory (higher Hurst exponent), so post-IPO price paths persist longer before correcting.

sources.role: finding: high initial and excess returns and heavy day-one turnover in Chinese IPOs, varying by industry
method and finding: R/S and ARFIMA estimates showing stronger long memory in Shenzhen than Shanghai

ideas.test: Collect A-share IPOs on both exchanges over a fixed window; compute first-day and 1-60 day market-adjusted abnormal returns; estimate a Hurst exponent per stock from its first 250 trading days; regress the speed of abnormal-return reversal on exchange, Hurst exponent, day-one turnover and industry controls.
ideas.disconfirming: No difference in reversal speed between exchanges, or Hurst exponent unrelated to the persistence of post-IPO abnormal returns once turnover and industry are controlled.

ideas.hypothesis: Listed construction, rolling-stock and local real estate firms earn positive abnormal returns around announcements of new tramway systems, and the size of the reaction is smaller when sell-side analysts disagree more about the firm's earnings.

sources.role: setting: a record number of new tramway systems scheduled to open, giving a set of announcement and opening events
measure: dispersion of sell-side analyst forecasts as a proxy for differences of opinion

ideas.test: Build an event list of tramway approval and contract-award announcements; identify listed contractors and suppliers named in them; run a market-model event study on (-1,+1) windows and interact abnormal returns with analyst forecast dispersion from I/B/E/S.
ideas.disconfirming: Cumulative abnormal returns indistinguishable from zero, or no moderation by analyst disagreement.

ideas.hypothesis: Large rolling-stock orders and leasing contracts announced by rail operators and manufacturers predict positive industry-level momentum in rail-equipment stocks over the following 3-12 months, similar to the industry-driven momentum found in Shanghai.

sources.role: mechanism: new rolling stock is a major capital outlay, often financed via leasing, creating large and lumpy order flows for suppliers and lessors
method and finding: momentum profits after costs and their dependence on industry

ideas.test: Compile dated rolling-stock order and lease announcements; form an industry index of rail-equipment manufacturers and lessors; test whether order value in month t predicts index excess returns in t+1 to t+12 controlling for market and standard momentum factors.
ideas.disconfirming: Order announcements carry no predictive power beyond past returns, or all reaction is complete within the announcement window.

ideas.hypothesis: Rail operators and manufacturers with high exposure to modernization programs have returns that co-move strongly with aggregate idiosyncratic volatility innovations and therefore earn lower expected returns than peers.

sources.role: mechanism and method: stocks correlated with aggregate idiosyncratic volatility innovations earn lower returns; portfolio and cross-sectional tests
setting: modernization decisions appraised with DCF under differing cost and efficiency assumptions, implying project-specific cash-flow uncertainty

ideas.test: Identify listed rail-related firms and a modernization-exposure measure (share of capex or contracts in modernization from annual reports); estimate each firm's beta to AIV innovations; test whether exposure predicts AIV beta and subsequent returns in Fama-MacBeth regressions.
ideas.disconfirming: Modernization exposure is unrelated to AIV beta, or high-AIV-beta rail firms do not earn lower returns.

ideas.hypothesis: Returns of large rail equipment manufacturers lead returns of small modernization-service suppliers after modernization contract news, and this lead-lag weakens when price limits bind.

sources.role: method: test of lead-lag relations between portfolio returns under price-limit restrictions
setting: modernization decisions that generate news relevant to both large OEMs and smaller refurbishers

ideas.test: Form daily portfolios of large and small rail-equipment stocks in a price-limit market; estimate VAR lead-lag coefficients overall and in windows around modernization contract news, adjusting for limit-hit days.
ideas.disconfirming: No significant lead of large over small portfolios around modernization news, matching the null in the price-limit study.

ideas.hypothesis: Shares of rolling-stock leasing companies respond to procurement announcements more slowly than shares of manufacturers, so lagged manufacturer returns predict lessor returns.

sources.role: method: lead-lag portfolio return tests
mechanism: leasing as an alternative procurement channel linking lessors' cash flows to new train orders

ideas.test: Daily return series for listed manufacturers and listed lessors or lessor parents; Granger causality and cross-autocorrelation tests, with event dummies for procurement announcements.
ideas.disconfirming: Lagged manufacturer returns have no predictive power for lessor returns, or lessors lead manufacturers.

ideas.hypothesis: Firms tied to tramway construction show overreaction: stocks with the largest gains during announcement years underperform, and the worst performers outperform over the next 2-3 years.

sources.role: setting: wave of new tramway openings as an attention-grabbing industry shock
method and finding: De Bondt-Thaler winner/loser portfolios showing overreaction

ideas.test: Construct winner and loser portfolios from construction and rail-supplier stocks ranked on returns during formation periods containing tramway announcements versus not; compare subsequent 24-36 month cumulative abnormal returns.
ideas.disconfirming: Loser-minus-winner returns are no larger after tramway-heavy formation periods than after other periods.

ideas.hypothesis: Momentum profits in stocks of firms headquartered in New Orleans are weaker in months following local public-safety shocks, because local investors trade less on past winners when local attention shifts.

sources.role: setting and measure: geocoded local incident data for New Orleans
method: momentum strategy construction with transaction-cost controls

ideas.test: Take firms headquartered in the New Orleans metro area; build monthly momentum returns; regress them on a local incident-rate index built from city crime and incident data, against a matched set of firms from other cities.
ideas.disconfirming: Local incident shocks do not change momentum profits for New Orleans firms relative to matched firms.

ideas.hypothesis: Firms with operations concentrated in New Orleans have higher sensitivity to aggregate idiosyncratic volatility innovations because local shocks are idiosyncratic, and so they earn lower average returns.

sources.role: mechanism and method: AIV-beta pricing in portfolio and cross-sectional tests
setting: city-specific local risk captured through GIS incident data

ideas.test: Identify firms with a high share of establishments in New Orleans; estimate their AIV betas; compare their returns with size and industry matched firms in Fama-MacBeth regressions.
ideas.disconfirming: AIV betas for New Orleans-concentrated firms equal those of matched firms, or no return difference.

ideas.hypothesis: Using concept mapping with researchers and practitioners to rank stock-return anomalies yields a priority ordering in which the top-ranked anomalies keep more of their out-of-sample return than lower-ranked ones.

sources.role: method: concept mapping to set a research agenda from researcher and practitioner input
setting: competing hypotheses about how differences of opinion affect returns, illustrating unresolved priorities

ideas.test: Survey a sample of academics and investment practitioners to rate about 30 published anomalies on importance and feasibility; cluster and rank them; compare post-publication returns of top-ranked and bottom-ranked anomalies.
ideas.disconfirming: Expert priority ranks are unrelated to, or negatively related to, post-publication anomaly returns.
